cited_details.statement: Modern deep neural networks have achieved remarkable performance in visual intelligence tasks such as image classification, object detection, and segmentation, but their accuracy typically scales with model capacity, parameter count, and computational cost [SOURCE 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531).
The resulting models are often too large to be deployed on resource-constrained devices such as smartphones, embedded systems, and edge sensors [SOURCE 16](https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v34i04.5963).

Knowledge distillation was popularized in its modern form by Hinton, Vinyals, and Dean, who proposed transferring the *soft predictions* of a large, well-trained "teacher" network to a smaller "student" network [SOURCE 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531).

In the canonical formulation, a *teacher* network—usually larger and pre-trained—is used to provide supervisory signals to a *student* network, which is the model that will actually be deployed [SOURCE 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531).
termed **"dark knowledge"** [SOURCE 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531).
- **Model compression.** Ensemble of large, deep teachers can be compressed into a single lightweight student suitable for embedded deployment [SOURCE 8](https://doi.org/10.3390/math8101652).

- **Improved generalization.** The teacher's soft targets provide a smoother supervisory signal that often regularizes the student and improves generalization beyond what is possible with hard labels alone [SOURCE 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531).

- **Cross-architecture knowledge transfer.** Distillation does not require the teacher and student to share an architecture, enabling knowledge to be transferred between heterogeneous networks [SOURCE 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6550).

- **Domain and modality transfer.** When a teacher is pre-trained on a different task, the visual priors it has learned can be transferred to the student via distillation [SOURCE 15](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.00261).

- **Capacity-gap alleviation.** A graduated sequence of intermediate "teacher assistants" can bridge the capacity gap between a very large teacher and a much smaller student, mitigating the performance degradation observed with single-step distillation [SOURCE 16](https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v34i04.5963).

introduced a temperature-softened softmax that produces a richer probability distribution over classes; the student is then trained to match this distribution via a (typically KL-divergence) distillation loss in addition to the cross-entropy loss with hard labels [SOURCE 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531).

Romero et al., in the **FitNets** framework, introduced the notion of *hints*—intermediate feature maps of the teacher that the student is encouraged to mimic through a regressor and a hint loss [SOURCE 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6550).

- **Attention-based feature matching.** Zagoruyko and Komodakis argued that *attention* over spatial or channel dimensions is a more compact and transferable form of intermediate knowledge than raw feature maps, and proposed attention transfer as a distillation objective [SOURCE 9](https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v35i9.16969).

More recent attention-based methods learn, rather than hand-design, the relative similarities between teacher and student features at all levels, controlling distillation intensities over all possible pairs of feature levels [SOURCE 9](https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v35i9.16969).

Semantic-calibrated cross-layer distillation (SemCKD) uses an attention mechanism to automatically assign, for each student layer, a distribution over teacher layers, allowing each student layer to distill knowledge from multiple teacher layers rather than a single fixed one [SOURCE 12](https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v35i8.16865).

ensemble feature-based, response-based, and relation-based lightweight knowledge distillation models, using a deeper teacher (e.g., ResNet-110) to train a much shallower student (e.g., ResNet-20) on classification tasks [SOURCE 8](https://doi.org/10.3390/math8101652).

The classical two-stage pipeline trains a teacher *first* (often as an ensemble), freezes it, and then trains the student to mimic the teacher's outputs and/or features [SOURCE 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531).

Offline single-teacher distillation remains the most widely used setting because it decouples teacher and student training, but it depends on having a sufficiently strong pre-trained teacher and can be limited by a large teacher–student capacity gap [SOURCE 16](https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v34i04.5963).

Because different teachers tend to make complementary errors, the ensemble carries richer knowledge than any single model, and a student trained against the ensemble can match or exceed the ensemble while remaining a single, deployable network [SOURCE 8](https://doi.org/10.3390/math8101652).

This intuition underlies "ensemble-then-distill" style multi-teacher frameworks, which first form a strong ensemble of teachers and then train a student against the ensemble's joint supervision [SOURCE 8](https://doi.org/10.3390/math8101652).

The On-the-Fly Native Ensemble (ONE) method trains a single multi-branch network that simultaneously establishes a strong teacher *on the fly* to enhance the target network's learning in a single training stage [SOURCE 14](https://qmro.qmul.ac.uk/xmlui/handle/123456789/58358).

ONE reports stronger generalization than alternative methods on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, and ImageNet while preserving computational efficiency [SOURCE 14](https://qmro.qmul.ac.uk/xmlui/handle/123456789/58358).

Furlanello et al., in **Born-Again Networks**, showed that a student of identical capacity to the teacher, trained with KD, can match the performance of the teacher ensemble, and that *replacing* the teacher with such re-trained students in turn can be iterated to further improve performance [SOURCE 5](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.04770).
The very name "Born-Again" reflects the discovery that a network "reborn" through distillation can match the ensemble it was distilled from [SOURCE 5](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.04770).

introduced a self-distillation scheme in which a CNN's deeper sections act as teachers for its shallower sections, so that the network trains auxiliary classifiers over intermediate features and distills knowledge from the deepest classifier back into the shallower ones [SOURCE 6](http://group.iiis.tsinghua.edu.cn/~maks/publications/pdf/Self-distillation.pdf).

- **Data-distortion guided self-distillation.** Rather than introducing a separate teacher, this approach trains a *single* network to be consistent across different distorted versions of the same training data, distilling knowledge across data views without reliance on an accompanying model [SOURCE 10](https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v33i01.33015565).
The method improves generalization on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet across architectures including AlexNet, ResNet, Wide ResNet, and DenseNet [SOURCE 10](https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v33i01.33015565).

observed that not all teachers distill equally well to a given student and proposed optimizing the teacher *to be easier for the student to learn from*, rather than simply maximizing its own accuracy [SOURCE 13](http://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07650).

showed that "the student network performance degrades when the gap between student and teacher is large" and that "a teacher can effectively transfer its knowledge to students up to a certain size, not smaller" [SOURCE 16](https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v34i04.5963).

Their solution is **multi-step knowledge distillation** with intermediate-sized *teacher-assistant* networks that bridge the gap, and they further studied the effect of teacher-assistant size and extended the framework to multiple assistants [SOURCE 16](https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v34i04.5963).

This insight is corroborated by later evolutionary-KD work, which explicitly contrasts the "small gap" and "big gap" regimes between teacher and student and seeks to address the latter [SOURCE 1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.13811).

**Student architecture search.** Rather than fixing a hand-designed student, Gu and Tresp focused on *the receiver* of the dark knowledge, i.e., the architecture of the student, and proposed searching for student architectures that better exploit the teacher's signal [SOURCE 11](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.11612).

**Evolutionary student–teacher search.** Evolutionary Knowledge Distillation addresses the fixed-teacher limitation of most distillation approaches by jointly evolving the student network and the distillation configuration, motivated by the observation that the teacher–student capacity gap strongly influences distillation outcomes [SOURCE 1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.13811).

Zhao and Wen presented a two-phase pipeline in which self-supervised learning supplies the teacher and knowledge distillation transfers its visual priors to the student [SOURCE 15](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.00261).

On the *knowledge* axis, the field has progressed from logits-based distillation [SOURCE 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531) to richer intermediate feature matching [SOURCE 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6550), attention-based representations [SOURCE 9](https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v35i9.16969), semantically calibrated cross-layer transfer [SOURCE 12](https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v35i8.16865), and relational signals [SOURCE 8](https://doi.org/10.3390/math8101652).

evidence.title: Show, Attend and Distill: Knowledge Distillation via Attention-based Feature Matching
evidence.abstract: Knowledge distillation extracts general knowledge from a pretrained teacher network and provides guidance to a target student network. Most studies manually tie intermediate features of the teacher and student, and transfer knowledge through predefined links. However, manual selection often constructs ineffective links that limit the improvement from the distillation. There has been an attempt to address the problem, but it is still challenging to identify effective links under practical scenarios. In this paper, we introduce an effective and efficient feature distillation method utilizing all the feature levels of the teacher without manually selecting the links. Specifically, our method utilizes an attention based meta network that learns relative similarities between features, and applies identified similarities to control distillation intensities of all possible pairs. As a result, our method determines competent links more efficiently than the previous approach and provides better performance on model compression and transfer learning tasks. evidence.title: Cross-Layer Distillation with Semantic Calibration
evidence.abstract: Recently proposed knowledge distillation approaches based on feature-map transfer validate that intermediate layers of a teacher model can serve as effective targets for training a student model to obtain better generalization ability. Existing studies mainly focus on particular representation forms for knowledge transfer between manually specified pairs of teacher-student intermediate layers. However, semantics of intermediate layers may vary in different networks and manual association of layers might lead to negative regularization caused by semantic mismatch between certain teacher-student layer pairs. To address this problem, we propose Semantic Calibration for Cross-layer Knowledge Distillation (SemCKD), which automatically assigns proper target layers of the teacher model for each student layer with an attention mechanism. With a learned attention distribution, each student layer distills knowledge contained in multiple layers rather than a single fixed intermediate layer from the teacher model for appropriate cross-layer supervision in training. Consistent improvements over state-of-the-art approaches are observed in extensive experiments with various network architectures for teacher and student models, demonstrating the effectiveness and flexibility of the proposed attention based soft layer association mechanism for cross-layer distillation.

evidence.title: Student Network Learning via Evolutionary Knowledge Distillation
evidence.abstract: Knowledge distillation provides an effective way to transfer knowledge via teacher-student learning, where most existing distillation approaches apply a fixed pre-trained model as teacher to supervise the learning of student network. This manner usually brings in a big capability gap between teacher and student networks during learning. Recent researches have observed that a small teacher-student capability gap can facilitate knowledge transfer. Inspired by that, we propose an evolutionary knowledge distillation approach to improve the transfer effectiveness of teacher knowledge. Instead of a fixed pre-trained teacher, an evolutionary teacher is learned online and consistently transfers intermediate knowledge to supervise student network learning on-the-fly. To enhance intermediate knowledge representation and mimicking, several simple guided modules are introduced between corresponding teacher-student blocks. In this way, the student can simultaneously obtain rich internal knowledge and capture its growth process, leading to effective student network learning. Extensive experiments clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach as well as good adaptability in the low-resolution and few-sample visual recognition scenarios.

evidence.title: Show, Attend and Distill: Knowledge Distillation via Attention-based Feature Matching
evidence.abstract: Knowledge distillation extracts general knowledge from a pretrained teacher network and provides guidance to a target student network. Most studies manually tie intermediate features of the teacher and student, and transfer knowledge through predefined links. However, manual selection often constructs ineffective links that limit the improvement from the distillation. There has been an attempt to address the problem, but it is still challenging to identify effective links under practical scenarios. In this paper, we introduce an effective and efficient feature distillation method utilizing all the feature levels of the teacher without manually selecting the links. Specifically, our method utilizes an attention based meta network that learns relative similarities between features, and applies identified similarities to control distillation intensities of all possible pairs. As a result, our method determines competent links more efficiently than the previous approach and provides better performance on model compression and transfer learning tasks. Further qualitative analyses and ablative studies describe how our method contributes to better distillation.

evidence.title: Ensemble Learning of Lightweight Deep Learning Models Using Knowledge Distillation for Image Classification
evidence.abstract: In recent years, deep learning models have been used successfully in almost every field including both industry and academia, especially for computer vision tasks. However, these models are huge in size, with millions (and billions) of parameters, and thus cannot be deployed on the systems and devices with limited resources (e.g., embedded systems and mobile phones). To tackle this, several techniques on model compression and acceleration have been proposed. As a representative type of them, knowledge distillation suggests a way to effectively learn a small student model from large teacher model(s). It has attracted increasing attention since it showed its promising performance. In the work, we propose an ensemble model that combines feature-based, response-based, and relation-based lightweight knowledge distillation models for simple image classification tasks. In our knowledge distillation framework, we use ResNet−20 as a student network and ResNet−110 as a teacher network. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed ensemble model outperforms other knowledge distillation models as well as the large teacher model for image classification tasks, with less computational power than the teacher model.

evidence.title: Search for Better Students to Learn Distilled Knowledge
evidence.abstract: Knowledge Distillation, as a model compression technique, has received great attention. The knowledge of a well-performed teacher is distilled to a student with a small architecture. The architecture of the small student is often chosen to be similar to their teacher's, with fewer layers or fewer channels, or both. However, even with the same number of FLOPs or parameters, the students with different architecture can achieve different generalization ability. The configuration of a student architecture requires intensive network architecture engineering. In this work, instead of designing a good student architecture manually, we propose to search for the optimal student automatically. Based on L1-norm optimization, a subgraph from the teacher network topology graph is selected as a student, the goal of which is to minimize the KL-divergence between student's and teacher's outputs. We verify the proposal on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 datasets. The empirical experiments show that the learned student architecture achieves better performance than ones specified manually. We also visualize and understand the architecture of the found student.
